recipe: Do not mutate preexisting variables or objects during component rendering; only return JSX.
trigger_condition: When writing the render logic of a React component.
evidence: React's rendering process must always be pure. Components should only *return* their JSX, and not *change* any objects or variables that existed before rendering—that would make them impure!

recipe: It is fine to mutate variables or objects that you create during the same render.
trigger_condition: When building arrays or objects inside a component's render function.
evidence: it's completely fine to change variables and objects that you've *just* created while rendering.

recipe: Place side effects in event handlers rather than in render logic.
trigger_condition: When your component needs to update the screen, start an animation, or change data in response to user interaction.
evidence: In React, **side effects usually belong inside [event handlers.](/learn/responding-to-events)** Event handlers are functions that React runs when you perform some action—for example, when you click a button. Even though event handlers are defined *inside* your component, they don't run *during* rendering! **So event handlers don't need to be pure.**

recipe: Use useEffect only as a last resort when a side effect cannot be expressed through an event handler.
trigger_condition: When a side effect does not fit naturally into an event handler.
evidence: If you've exhausted all other options and can't find the right event handler for your side effect, you can still attach it to your returned JSX with a [`useEffect`](/reference/react/useEffect) call in your component. This tells React to execute it later, after rendering, when side effects are allowed. **However, this approach should be your last resort.**

recipe: Treat props, state, and context as read-only during rendering; use setState to update state instead of mutating.
trigger_condition: When you need to update a component's state in response to user input.
evidence: You should always treat these inputs as read-only. When you want to *change* something in response to user input, you should [set state](/learn/state-a-components-memory) instead of writing to a variable. You should never change preexisting variables or objects while your component is rendering.

recipe: Do not depend on the rendering order of sibling components; each component should calculate its JSX independently.
trigger_condition: When writing a component that might interact with or depend on other components' rendering sequence.
evidence: In general, you should not expect your components to be rendered in any particular order.

recipe: Calculate the value you need (e.g., a className) and include it in your render output instead of mutating the DOM directly during rendering.
trigger_condition: When a component needs to set a DOM attribute like className based on a condition during the render phase.
evidence: In this example, the side effect (modifying the DOM) was not necessary at all. You only needed to return JSX.

recipe: Pass data between components via props rather than using module-level variables, because React does not guarantee the execution order of component functions.
trigger_condition: When multiple components need to access the same data and you are tempted to share it through a variable defined outside the components.
evidence: Remember that React does not guarantee that component functions will execute in any particular order, so you can't communicate between them by setting variables. All communication must happen through props.

recipe: Do not mutate a prop (such as calling push on an array prop) during rendering, as it mutates an object created before your component started rendering and causes unpredictable behavior.
trigger_condition: When you need to modify a prop like an array to add items before rendering the component.
evidence: By calling `push` on the received `stories` array (a prop!), it is mutating an object that was created *before* `StoryTray` started rendering. This makes it buggy and very difficult to predict.

recipe: Keep state mutations local to event handlers or effects so your component's rendering function stays pure.
trigger_condition: You are updating state in a React component and want to maintain a pure render function.
evidence: This keeps your mutation local and your rendering function pure.

recipe: When updating an existing item in an array state, clone that item rather than mutating it in place.
trigger_condition: You need to change a specific element within an array held in React state.
evidence: if you tried to change any of the array's existing items, you'd have to clone those items too.

recipe: Prefer non-mutating array operations (slice, filter, map) over mutating ones (push, pop, reverse, sort) when updating array state, since the latter modify the original array in place.
trigger_condition: You are updating an array in React state and need to choose between mutating and non-mutating array methods.
evidence: `push`, `pop`, `reverse`, and `sort` will mutate the original array, but `slice`, `filter`, and `map` will create a new one.
